To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we have developed a new model that can be used to study the evolution of the stellar mass function of galaxies in the early Universe, (2) this model is able to reproduce the evolution of the galaxy stellar mass function in a wide redshift range (0<z<3) for a variety of galaxy types and masses, (3) the model can be used to make predictions of the evolution of the cold gas mass function and of the star formation rate, and (4) the

the high-redshift overproduction of stars in modeled dwarf galaxies can be mitigated with three empirical adjustments of star formation recipes: (1) increasing the efficiency of gas accretion, (2) increasing the efficiency with which stellar feedback is mass loaded, and (3), to a lesser extent, decreasing the efficiency with which gas is turned into stars.

the three physical scenarios we consider are able to reproduce observed galaxy evolution, and the best scenario is one where the efficiency of star-forming gas is reduced in low-mass galaxies at high redshift.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the observed properties of the Milky Way and the LMC are consistent with their formation by a major merger of two galaxies with masses similar to those of the two galaxies.
there are no convincing arguments that can be used to explain the observed properties of the high-redshift universe in the framework of the standard model of cosmology.

, although the current models are not able to reproduce all of the observed properties of galaxies at high redshifts, the current models do not rule out the possibility of the existence of the observed properties.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the high redshift overproduction problem is a problem of the gas physics, and not the star formation physics.
we have shown that the high-redshift overproduction of stars in modeled dwarf galaxies is a result of the gas accretion rate being too tightly coupled with the star formation rate in the models.
we have found a solution to the problem of overproduction of stars at high redshifts in low-mass galaxies, by decoupling gas accretion from star formation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the high-redshift star formation problem is likely a result of gas accretion being too efficient, which could be caused by a variety of physical effects.
the high-redshift overproduction of stars in low-mass galaxies is a fundamental problem for semi-analytic models that is not easily solved by modifying standard recipes.

the star formation histories of low-mass galaxies are sensitive to the details of the gas accretion process, and that a more detailed treatment of this process is needed in order to match the evolution of low-mass galaxy stellar masses and star formation rates.
